For <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2 \le \theta \le \pi</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 + \theta \ge 3</annotation></semantics></math>, so the spiral is the outer boundary: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>θ</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}\int_2^{\pi} \left((1 + \theta)^2 - 3^2\right)d\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: This subtracts the wrong way: for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta > 2</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>></mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 + \theta > 3</annotation></semantics></math>, so the spiral is outside.

Right: after <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta = 2</annotation></semantics></math> the spiral is the outer curve.

That squares the difference of the radii, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1 + \theta) - 3</annotation></semantics></math>; square each radius, then subtract.

The <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> from the wedge area is missing.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>θ</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}\int_2^{\pi} \left((1 + \theta)^2 - 9\right)d\theta</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">≈</mo><mn>2.203</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 2.203</annotation></semantics></math> (calculator).

Setting <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>-values equal finds crossings reached at the same <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. A point has many polar names, and the pole is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 0</annotation></semantics></math> at every angle, so always check where each curve reaches the pole.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = \sin\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is 0 at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta = 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = \cos\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is 0 at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>: both pass through the pole.
That is what the equation finds, but two curves can also meet at a point named by different polar coordinates, like the pole.

At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{5\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> both <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>-values are <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>: the same point as at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, not the pole.

Right: a crossing at the pole need not happen at the same <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, so check <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = 0</annotation></semantics></math> on each curve.
